title: Wiggins Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Wiggins wells have a 154-foot median depth; finished well costs at that depth model at $13,700-$22,800.
h1: Wiggins, Colorado Well Depths, Yields, and Costs
intro_html:
Well records around Wiggins show a mostly consistent plains drilling profile, but the permit database is not complete for every measurement. Of 937 permitted wells within 5 miles, 509 are recorded as constructed, 570 report total depth, 272 report pump yield, and only 28 report static water level. That makes the depth data more useful for estimating a bid than the yield data is for guaranteeing household performance.

Most recorded wells are in the Denver Basin aquifer system and the surrounding area includes Orchard, Jackson Lake, Weldona, and Log Lane Village. Before buying land, review nearby well permits, confirm the intended use, and have a driller evaluate the specific parcel.

sections.heading: Wiggins well depth: mostly shallow to moderate
sections.html:
The median recorded well depth near Wiggins is 154 feet. The middle half runs from 125 to 187 feet, and the 90th percentile is 220 feet. That gives a driller a practical starting range for a preliminary bid, but not a guaranteed completion depth.

Depths are concentrated in the 100-to-300-foot range, which accounts for 92% of the depth mix. Another 7% are under 100 feet. The deepest record is 645 feet, so unusual conditions do occur even though the local pattern is much shallower. Permits identify Denver Basin aquifer wells in 95% of the records, with Quaternary Alluvium and Alluvial entries also present. Ask what casing and grout design the driller expects at your lot.

sections.heading: What Wiggins wells produce
sections.html:
Reported pump yields are unusually strong on paper: the median is 587.5 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 15.0 to 1200.0 gallons per minute. The recorded mix shows 95% above 15 gallons per minute, 5% between 5 and 15, and none under 5.

Those figures apply to only 272 wells and are reported pump yields, not a promise of sustained household supply. A buyer should ask for the well completion report, pump test information, and any restrictions tied to the permit. Domestic and household wells make up 42% of the use mix, while stock and irrigation records account for 27% and 35%. Irrigation capacity does not automatically establish unrestricted domestic use.

sections.heading: Water levels around Wiggins
sections.html:
Only 28 wells report a static water level, so the local water-level sample is limited. Among those records, the median depth to water is 96 feet, with the middle half from 76 to 103 feet. That is useful for discussing pump placement and initial site expectations, but it is not enough to establish a water-table trend across Wiggins.

The permit counts by decade also do not provide a water-level-by-decade series. They show permitting activity, not whether the water table is rising or falling. Have the driller check current nearby records and measure the completed well before selecting the pump. A static level can differ from the pumping level, so the pump system should be sized from actual testing rather than the median alone.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Wiggins, and when
sections.html:
Permit records extend from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The largest decade counts are 104 permits in the 1990s, 96 in the 1970s, 92 in the 2000s, 88 in the 2020s, 85 in the 1960s, 64 in the 1980s, 48 in the 2010s, and 47 in the 1950s. These counts show long-term drilling activity, not current availability or well success.

The most active names in the records are Canfield, Leslie George, with 143 wells; Canfield Drilling Company, listed as Canfield, Harold E, with 87; and Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 56. Treat these as permit-history names, then independently confirm licensing, insurance, schedule, references, and the scope of any current proposal.

sections.heading: Estimated cost to drill a Wiggins well
sections.html:
The cost model for Wiggins assumes Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock and a drilling rate of $50 to $70 per foot. At the 154-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $7,700 to $10,800.

A finished system, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, models at about $13,700 to $22,800 at that median depth. The final price can move outside that range if the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs additional electrical or trench work. Get the bid broken into drilling, casing, grouting, testing, pump equipment, trenching, and electrical rather than comparing one lump sum.

sections.heading: Wiggins risks to check before closing
sections.html:
Yield is not the only concern. The mapped area within about 10 miles contains 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. There are no recorded historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in that mapped set, but a map is not a substitute for testing the water from the specific well.

Ask for a current laboratory test, the well construction report, and any nearby environmental information. Confirm the septic location and replacement area can meet applicable separation and soil requirements. A low-yield or unsuccessful hole can still create a substantial cost, even though the recorded yield distribution near Wiggins is strong. Also verify that the permit allows the intended household, stock, or irrigation use. New construction may require an augmentation plan in an over-appropriated basin, so confirm water rights before buying land.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Wiggins lot
sections.html:
Start with the permits nearest the parcel, not just the countywide reputation. Compare recorded depths, reported yields, aquifer descriptions, use types, and construction dates from Wiggins toward Orchard, Jackson Lake, Weldona, and Log Lane Village. Neighboring wells can help a driller frame the proposal, but they do not guarantee the same result at a new location.

Before closing, make the purchase contract depend on confirming the well permit, legal water use, septic feasibility, access for a rig, and a realistic drilling allowance. For a homesite, budget the complete system rather than the drilled hole alone. If the property is intended for irrigation or stock, have the water-rights and permit conditions reviewed separately from the household supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Wiggins, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Wiggins is 154 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 125 to 187 feet, while the 90th percentile is 220 feet. Most wells, 92%, fall between 100 and 300 feet, but the deepest record is 645 feet. A nearby permit is useful for estimating, not guaranteeing, a new depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Wiggins?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 154-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at $7,700 to $10,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work models at $13,700 to $22,800. A deeper hole, difficult access, or extra site work can change the proposal.

faq.q: How much water do Wiggins wells produce?
faq.a: Among 272 records reporting pump yield, the median is 587.5 gallons per minute. The middle half ranges from 15.0 to 1200.0 gallons per minute, and 95% report more than 15 gallons per minute. These are recorded pump yields, not guaranteed sustained production. Review the completion report and testing for the specific well.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Wiggins, Colorado?
faq.a: The mapped area within about 10 miles has 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites. That does not establish contamination at a particular well, and there are no mapped EPA Superfund or cleanup sites in the facts provided. Test the well through a laboratory and review nearby environmental information before relying on it for household use.

faq.q: Do Wiggins wells have a stable water table?
faq.a: Only 28 nearby well records report static water level. Those records show a median depth to water of 96 feet, with the middle half from 76 to 103 feet. The available facts do not include a water-level-by-decade series, so they do not support calling the water table rising or falling. Have the completed well measured and tested.
